analysis.one_liner: Makes packaging and beverage companies pay to collect and recycle their plastic waste and phases out many single-use plastics.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: introduced in March 2021 with 14 Senate cosponsors, it got no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would shift the cost of dealing with packaging and plastic waste from taxpayers and local governments to the companies that make and sell the products. It would require producers to join organizations that fund collection, recycling, and composting; put at least a 10-cent refundable deposit on most beverage containers; phase out items like single-use plastic bags, utensils, and styrofoam food service products; force plastic bottles to contain growing shares of recycled material; pause new permits for plastic manufacturing plants until pollution rules catch up; standardize recycling labels nationwide; and restrict exporting plastic waste to other countries. Companies with under $1 million in annual revenue would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and communities that live with plastic litter, microplastics in water and food, and recycling confusion, plus local governments and taxpayers who currently foot the bill for waste management and litter cleanup. Small businesses under $1 million in revenue are carved out of the producer-responsibility fees, and people with disabilities can still get plastic straws on request.

how_it_helps.text: Producers of packaging, paper, single-use products, and beverage containers would become financially responsible for collecting, managing, and recycling or composting them after consumer use, instead of cities and taxpayers.
The bill sets rising minimum percentages of products that must be reused, recycled, or composted, and requires beverage containers to contain increasing shares of recycled material.
It phases out a range of single-use plastic products starting January 1, 2023, bans single-use plastic carryout bags, and puts a refundable deposit of at least 10 cents on most beverage containers.
It places a temporary moratorium on new or expanded permits for certain plastics manufacturing facilities until regulations address pollution from those facilities.
It requires standardized, easy-to-read recycling and composting labels nationwide and limits the export of plastic waste to other countries.
Companies with less than $1 million in annual revenue, and responsible parties handling under one ton of covered products a year, are exempt from the producer-responsibility program.

analysis.who_pays: Large beverage, packaging, consumer-goods, and plastics companies would bear new fees, deposits, recycled-content mandates, and design requirements. Some of those costs would likely show up in slightly higher shelf prices, and retailers would have to handle container returns and drop single-use plastic bags and utensils.

drawbacks.text: Producer fees and deposit requirements would be passed at least partly to consumers through higher prices, and a national 10-cent bottle deposit adds a new errand for shoppers who do not return containers.

The bill exempts producer responsibility organizations and their members from antitrust law when carrying out their approved plans, letting competitors coordinate pricing and program decisions under a federal umbrella.

Retailers and restaurants would have to accept returned containers and pay refunds (with daily per-person caps), a real administrative burden for smaller stores even with the under-$1-million exemption.
The single-use bans rest heavily on EPA determinations of what is 'recyclable' or 'compostable,' which could shift with administrations and create compliance uncertainty for food service businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: companies that profit from single-use packaging would pay for its cleanup, and plastic waste and litter would fall, at the price of modestly higher consumer prices and new compliance work for retailers and food service. The main design soft spots are the antitrust exemption for producer organizations and reliance on EPA discretion. On balance the benefits to communities and municipal budgets outweigh those costs, though the transition would be bumpy for small retailers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on March 25, 2021, with ten original cosponsors including Sens. Booker, Durbin, Markey, Wyden, Warren, Sanders, and Feinstein.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.
Fourteen senators cosponsored the bill in total: 13 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and 1 of its 2 independents; no Republican did.
The bill received no committee markup, no hearing listed in the action history, and no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastics, packaging, and beverage manufacturers are better off: they avoided the fees, deposit obligations, recycled-content mandates, and permit moratorium the bill would have imposed, while cities and taxpayers continue paying for waste management as before.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Break Free From Plastic Pollution Act of 2021 on March 25, 2021.

against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the Break Free From Plastic Pollution Act, objecting to the plastics facility permit moratorium and single-use phase-outs.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were Democrats or independents — 13 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents — and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll call exists.

industries.note: The bill would pause new or expanded permits for certain plastics facilities until pollution rules are updated and would phase out many single-use plastic products, directly constraining the industry's growth. Its waste becomes the industry's financial problem rather than a public one.

A national refundable deposit of at least 10 cents per container and mandates rising to 80 percent recycled content by 2040 would add costs across nearly every bottled drink. Consumers get refunds back, so the money flows through, but compliance falls on the companies.

Producers would pay fees covering collection, recycling, composting, and even litter cleanup of their products, ending the arrangement in which cities absorb those costs. Companies under $1 million in revenue are exempt.

Stores and restaurants would have to collect and refund beverage container deposits, stop providing plastic bags and utensils by default, and face federal fines for violations — but small businesses are exempt from the heaviest requirements and states with similar laws can get waivers.

Producer fees would fund collection, sorting, composting, and new recycling infrastructure, with a mandate that half of program spending in the first ten years go to building that infrastructure — a large new revenue stream for recyclers and haulers.
Cities currently pay to manage packaging waste they did not create; the bill shifts that cost to producers and requires reporting on resulting reductions in state and local taxes.
